China's 2-Month Opposition Window: A Trademark Watch SOP for Foreign Brands

Article 36 of the 2026 Trademark Law cuts the opposition window from three months to two. For foreign brands, that turns an occasional register check into an operational process with named owners and pre-authorised counsel.

Why Two Months Changes the Whole Chain

Article 36 of the revised PRC Trademark Law, effective 1 January 2027, sets the opposition period at two months from the date of preliminary publication (down from three under Article 33 of the 2019 law). The period runs from publication, not from when your team happens to notice the application.

Under Article 4 of the CNIPA's draft transition measures, the dividing line is the publication date: the Trademark Gazette date for domestic applications and the WIPO publication date for international registrations designating China. Marks published before 1 January 2027 keep the 3-month window; those published on or after it get 2 months. A window that straddles the year boundary is not restarted.

The practical consequence is that detection, internal approval, evidence collection, translation, notarisation where required and local counsel instruction all have to complete inside eight weeks. A brand that reviews the register quarterly will lose the right to oppose before it finishes its first internal meeting.

Draft status: the transition measures were open for comment until 12 November 2026 and may change. Confirm the final text before setting hard internal deadlines.

A Backwards Timeline From Publication Day

PointActionOwner
Weekly, continuouslyGazette watch runs on core classes, sub-classes and Chinese-character variants; alerts go to a named inbox, not a shared distribution list with no ownerWatch provider / IP counsel
Day 0–2Publication detected; conflict scored (identical, near-identical, transliteration, related company or distributor)IP counsel
Day 3–5Go / no-go decision under a pre-agreed threshold; budget released automatically for high-risk conflictsBrand owner (pre-authorised)
Day 6–14Evidence pack assembled, foreign-language documents translated, signature and authorisation obtainedLocal agent + brand owner
Day 15–30Opposition filed electronically; reserve the right to submit supplementary evidenceChinese trademark agency
BufferKeep at least four weeks unused for holidays, courier delays, document legalisation and internal escalationProgramme owner

Filing on day 55 is technically possible but leaves no margin. The point of the SOP is to make the decision, not the filing, the bottleneck.

Watch Configuration Checklist

  • Marks: the Latin word mark, the official Chinese name, common transliterations, consumer-coined nicknames, pinyin, abbreviations, device marks and the Chinese name of each product line.
  • Scope: the classes you registered, adjacent classes you may enter, the specific CNIPA sub-classes you use, and the classes where squatters commonly file (often 9, 25, 35, 41, 43 depending on sector).
  • Parties: your own entity names, distributors, former agents, OEM factories and known squatters — a filing by a former partner is easier to challenge when the relationship is documented.
  • Frequency: weekly at minimum; daily or near-real-time alerts for your top three classes. Monthly sampling is not compatible with a 2-month statutory window.
  • Escalation: one named decision-maker, a deputy, a pre-signed power of attorney on file with your Chinese agent, and a standing instruction to file a protective opposition when the deadline is within ten working days.
  • Records: log the publication date, the alert date, the decision and the filing receipt. These dates matter if the other side later argues the opposition was out of time.

For the broader monitoring framework, see our trademark monitoring and protection guide.

The Evidence Pack to Keep Ready

An opposition is won on documents, not on the fact that your brand is well known. Keep a standing, refreshed pack so that only the conflicting application needs to be added:

  • Proof of your prior rights: home-country registrations, Chinese registrations, earlier applications and priority documents.
  • Proof of reputation in China: dated advertising, media coverage, trade-fair presence, e-commerce listings, distributor agreements and sales records showing use before the conflicting filing date.
  • Proof of the applicant's bad faith: a pattern of filings resembling other brands, prior business contact, an offer to sell the mark back, or a filing by a distributor or manufacturer.
  • Identity and authorisation documents: an up-to-date power of attorney and corporate registration extracts, with translations ready.

Filing mechanics matter. CNIPA's official FAQ on electronic oppositions states that evidence uploaded through the online system must be in PDF, that the "legal and factual grounds" field in an electronic opposition is limited to 2,000 characters, and that supplementary evidence is only possible if you selected the option to reserve that right when filing — in which case it must be submitted within three months. An opposition respondent has 30 days to reply; supplementary evidence must be declared in the reply and filed within three months of it.

After Filing: What the Calendar Looks Like

StageTiming / rule
Opposition examinationCNIPA decides within 12 months of the end of the publication period, extendable by 6 months (Art. 38)
Respondent's reply30 days from receipt of the notice (CNIPA electronic-filing FAQ)
Supplementary evidenceDeclare in the submission and file within 3 months; PDF only (CNIPA FAQ)
Stay of proceedingsArt. 41 allows suspension where the outcome depends on another pending case — useful when the cited prior right is itself under invalidation
AppealA party dissatisfied with the opposition decision may request review within 15 days (Art. 38)

Budget for CNIPA official fees, local agent fees, translation and, where needed, notarisation or an Apostille. Fee schedules change; confirm the current amounts with your agent rather than relying on third-party summaries.

Five Failure Modes We See Repeatedly

  1. Monitoring only the Latin mark, so an opposition is missed when a squatter files the Chinese transliteration.
  2. Relying on distributors or customers to report a conflict informally.
  3. Waiting for head-office approval with no pre-agreed threshold or deputy.
  4. Discovering the power of attorney has expired or the registered address has changed.
  5. Treating the 2-month period as if a court-style extension were available. It is a statutory window, not a negotiable deadline.

The cheapest fix is procedural: pre-authorise your agent, log publication dates, and run the watch weekly. See the full pre-2027 action list for the other four workstreams.

Sources and Caveats

Primary sources: Articles 36, 38 and 41 of the Trademark Law of the PRC (2026 Revision) (CNIPA, 26 June 2026); CNIPA notice of 28 September 2026 on the draft transition measures; CNIPA Trademark Office, FAQ on Electronic Applications for Opposition, Non-Use Cancellation and Invalidation. Draft measures are not final. This is general information, not legal advice.
